chapters.title: Subject-Verb Agreement & Sentence Foundations
chapters.summary: The building blocks of a sentence and the eight agreement cases that decide your mark. The single highest-value, lowest-effort accuracy gain in the whole exam.

blocks.text: Before any IELTS-specific technique, your sentences have to be mechanically sound. This module fixes the four faults that quietly lower your score on every single line of your writing and speaking: verbs that do not agree with their subjects, tenses that put events in the wrong time, missing or misused articles, and wrong prepositions. None of these is difficult. All of them are habits. Module 1 turns the correct habit into your default, so that by Module 2 you can build ambitious sentences on a base that does not leak marks.
blocks.bn: মডিউল ১-এর লক্ষ্য: ব্যান্ড ৬ পার হতে হলে আগে বাক্যের ভিত্তি নির্ভুল হতে হবে। এই মডিউল সেই চারটি মৌলিক ভুল ঠিক করে যা প্রতিটি বাক্যে নম্বর কমায়: subject-verb agreement, tense, article, ও preposition।

blocks.text: 1.1 First, the building blocks (start here even if you think you know)

This book assumes you know nothing, so we begin with the parts of a sentence. You do not need to memorise these labels to speak Bangla, but almost every rule in this book is stated using them, so learn to recognise them.
Every basic English sentence has two essential parts and often a third:

items: The subject is the person or thing the sentence is about, the one that does the action. In “Students study hard,” the subject is students.
The verb is the action or the state of being. In “Students study hard,” the verb is study. The verb be (is, am, are, was, were) shows a state rather than an action: “The graph is clear.”
The object is the person or thing that receives the action. In “Students use the internet,” the object is the internet.

blocks.text: The normal English order is Subject + Verb + Object (S + V + O). Students (S) use (V) the internet (O).

blocks.title: Regional Tip (Bangla speakers)
blocks.text: Bangla is a Subject-Object-Verb language. আমি ভাত খাই is literally “I rice eat,” with the verb at the very end. English puts the verb second, right after the subject: “I eat rice.” When an English sentence you write feels wrong, the first thing to check is whether the verb has drifted to the end out of Bangla habit.

“Agreement” simply means matching. Subject-verb agreement is the rule that the verb must match its subject in number. A singular subject (one) takes one form of the verb; a plural subject (more than one) takes another. That is the entire idea. The rest of this chapter is about the cases where spotting the true subject is tricky.
1.2 The core rule
In the present simple tense, the verb changes depending on whether the subject is singular or plural.
Notice the trap that catches thousands of Bangladeshi candidates: the -s is reversed between nouns and verbs.

items: On a noun, -s means plural: one student, many students.
On a verb, -s means singular: he works, they work.

blocks.text: So a correct sentence often has an -s on either the noun or the verb, but not both: The student works. (singular noun, verb takes -s) / The students work. (plural noun, verb has no -s)
blocks.bn: noun-এ -s মানে বহুবচন, কিন্তু verb-এ -s মানে একবচন। এই উল্টো নিয়মই সবচেয়ে বেশি ভুলের কারণ। “The student works” আর “The students work”, দুটোর একতিতে -s থাকে।

blocks.text: The verb be and have are irregular and must be memorised:
The result is clear. / The results are clear. The number has risen. / The numbers have risen.
1.3 The cases that actually decide your mark

The core rule is easy. Marks are lost on the cases below, where the true subject is hidden, disguised, or further away from the verb than a nearer noun. Master these eight and you remove almost every agreement error from your writing.
Case 1 · Words between the subject and the verb
The verb agrees with the true subject, never with the nearest noun. Writers are pulled toward the closest word, which is usually wrong.

blocks.incorrect: The list of items are on the table.
blocks.correct: The list of items is on the table.
blocks.why: The subject is “list” (singular), not “items”. Cross out the middle phrase and the truth is obvious: “The list … is.”

blocks.incorrect: The quality of the answers were poor.
blocks.correct: The quality of the answers was poor.

blocks.text: Technique: find the subject, then mentally delete every word between it and the verb. “The list of items is.”
Case 2 · “The number of” versus “a number of”
This pair appears constantly in Writing Task 1, and the two behave in opposite ways.

items: “The number of + plural noun” takes a singular verb (the subject is number, one figure).
“A number of + plural noun” takes a plural verb (it simply means several).

blocks.text: The number of tourists has increased since 2010. / A number of tourists were waiting outside the museum.
Case 3 · Collective nouns
Words such as government, team, committee, family, company, public, staff name a group. In IELTS academic writing, treat each as a single unit and use a singular verb.
The government is planning three new policies. / The committee has reached a decision.

(British English sometimes allows a plural verb when the focus is on the individual members: “the team are arguing among themselves.” For IELTS academic Writing, stay singular and consistent. It is safer and never wrong.)
Case 4 · Indefinite pronouns are singular
Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, anyone, nobody, either, neither, one are all singular, however plural the words around them look.
Each of the students has a laptop. (not “have”) / Everyone in the classes was present. / Neither of the options is acceptable.
blocks.bn: each of, every, everyone সবসময় singular, পরে যত বড় বহুবচন noun-ই থাকুক না কেন।

blocks.text: Case 5 · “Neither…nor,” “either…or,” “not only…but also”
With these paired connectors, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the one closest to the verb.

Neither the manager nor the employees were informed. (nearer subject: employees, plural) / Neither the employees nor the manager was informed. (nearer subject: manager, singular) / Not only the students but also the teacher was worried.
Case 6 · Compound subjects joined by “and”
Two subjects joined by and are almost always plural.
The teacher and the students were in the hall. / Poverty and unemployment remain serious problems.
Exception: when the two words describe a single combined thing, treat them as singular: “Bread and butter is a common breakfast.” This is rare in IELTS.
Case 7 · “There is” and “there are”
After there, the verb agrees with the real subject, which comes after the verb.
There is a serious problem. (subject: problem, singular) / There are several factors. (subject: factors, plural) / There is a range of options. (subject: range, singular)
Case 8 · Uncountable nouns, amounts, and inverted structures

Uncountable nouns are treated as singular and never take a plural -s. Memorise the high-frequency IELTS set as a block: information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, water, work.

blocks.incorrect: The informations are correct and he gave many advices.
blocks.correct: The information is correct and he gave a lot of advice.

blocks.text: Amounts of time, money, and distance are treated as a single quantity, so they take a singular verb. Ten years is a long time to wait. / Five thousand taka is not enough.

Inverted structures (where the verb comes before the subject) still agree with the subject. When a sentence begins with a negative adverb such as not only or hardly, find the subject after the verb and match it. Hardly ever does the government reverse such a decision. / Only after 2010 did the figures begin to fall.
(You will meet inversion in full in Chapter 8. Here, only notice that agreement still applies.)

blocks.title: Why Bangla speakers make agreement mistakes
blocks.body: Almost every subject-verb agreement error you make traces back to one fact: the Bangla verb does not change its ending to match a singular or plural subject the way the English verb does. The verb form যায় (jay) is identical for “he” and for “they.” Bangla marks person and formality, but it does not force the singular-plural switch on the verb that English demands. Because your first language never trained this switch, your ear does not warn you when it is missing.

error_types.label: Error type 1 · The dropped third-person -s. Because Bangla adds no -s, learners write the base verb everywhere.
error_types.incorrect: He go to the market every day. / The population increase rapidly.
error_types.correct: He goes to the market every day. / The population increases rapidly.

error_types.label: Error type 2 · The dropped or wrong “is / are.” Bangla often has no separate word for is in a simple statement (সে ভালো = “he good”), so learners drop it or pick the wrong number.
error_types.incorrect: Many people is using the internet. / The graph show that pollution have increased.
error_types.correct: Many people are using the internet. / The graph shows that pollution has increased.

blocks.bn: বাংলা verb singular/plural অনুযায়ী বদলায় না (সে যায় / তারা যায়, একই রূপ)। তাই ইংরেজিতে -s বাদ পড়া আর is/are ভুল হওয়া সবচেয়ে সাধারণ। কানে ধরা যাবে না, তাই লেখার পর ইচ্ছা করে প্রতিটি verb মিলিয়ে দেখতে হবে।

blocks.title: Why this one rule caps your band
blocks.body: Subject-verb agreement is the error examiners notice first, because it appears in the very first line of almost every answer and it repeats. A script with recurring agreement errors cannot reach Band 7 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy, however good the ideas are, because the criterion at Band 7 requires that the majority of sentences are error-free. One agreement slip per sentence removes that. The damage is heaviest in Writing Task 1, which lives on subjects like the number of, the proportion of, the figure for, every one of which is singular. Fixing agreement is the single highest-value, lowest-effort accuracy gain in the whole exam.

examples.Task 1: The number of visitors has risen sharply, whereas the proportion of local tourists has fallen.
examples.Task 2: Although the government provides free healthcare, demand continues to outstrip supply.
examples.Speaking Part 2: My family lives in a small town, and each of my brothers has a different job.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 1. Chapter 2 (Tense Mastery & Time Precision) follows.

chapters.title: Tense Mastery & Time Precision
chapters.summary: The twelve tenses mapped, the five that IELTS rewards, and the two critical pairs (past simple vs present perfect, present simple vs present continuous) that cause almost all tense errors.

blocks.text: Subject-verb agreement made your verbs match. Tense makes them sit in the right time. In IELTS this is not a small point of grammar; it is a matter of meaning. Writing Task 1 describes data that already happened or is happening now, Task 2 predicts and generalises, and Speaking moves constantly between past stories and future plans. Put a verb in the wrong time and you have not just made a grammar slip, you have said something untrue about when it happened. That is why examiners treat tense control as a core signal of the Band 6-to-7 jump.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ২-এর মূল কথা: tense মানে verb-কে সঠিক সময়ে বসানো। ভুল tense মানে শুধু grammar ভুল নয়, ঘটনাটা কখন ঘটলো সেটাই ভুল বলা। IELTS-এ এটি নম্বর কাটার বড় কারণ।

blocks.text: 2.1 What a tense actually is (zero assumption)
An English tense carries two pieces of information at once:

items: Time: past, present, or future. (When did it happen?)
Aspect: simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous. (Is it a whole finished event, an action in progress, an action linked to another time, or a mix?)

blocks.text: Three times multiplied by four aspects gives the twelve tenses. That sounds like a lot, but the good news for IELTS is that five of them do about 90 per cent of the work, and this chapter foregrounds those five while still showing you the full map so nothing is a mystery.
The four aspects, in plain words:

rows: a whole event, a fact, a habit
an action linked to a later time; “before now / before then”
an action in progress up to a point, with duration

blocks.text: 2.2 The complete map of the twelve tenses
Study the whole table once so you can recognise every form. Then move to 2.3, where we foreground the five that matter most.

rows: past action still relevant; trend up to now
duration of an action continuing to now
Prices have been rising for a decade.
finished event at a finished time
action in progress at a past moment
Sales were falling when the law changed.
an earlier past action before another past action
duration up to a point in the past
It had been raining for hours before it stopped.
Demand will rise over the next decade.
action in progress at a future moment
By 2030, most cars will be running on electricity.
an action completed before a future point
By 2040, the city will have doubled in size.
duration up to a future point
By June she will have been working here for ten years.

blocks.text: p.p. = past participle (the third form: go / went / gone; rise / rose / risen). The high-frequency irregular list is in Appendix A at the back of the book. Learn it as fixed items, the way you learned vocabulary.
2.3 The five tenses IELTS actually rewards
You can describe any graph and answer any Speaking question accurately with these five. Master them before you worry about the rest.

items: Present simple for facts, habits, general truths, and Task 2 positions.
Present continuous for what is happening now and for current trends.
Past simple for finished events and historical graph data.
Present perfect for actions and trends that reach up to the present.
Future (will / going to) for predictions and plans.

blocks.text: Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors. The rest of the chapter drills those two pairs, because fixing them fixes most of your tense marks.
2.4 Critical pair 1 · Past simple versus present perfect
This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it is decisive in Task 1.

items: Use the past simple when the time is finished, and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago, between 2000 and 2010.
Use the present perfect when the action reaches up to now, or when the exact time does not matter: signalled by since, for, over the past decade, recently, so far, already.

blocks.text: Past simple: The population rose in 2010. (a finished year) / Present perfect: The population has risen since 2010. (2010 up to the present)
The clearest signal is the time word:

headers: Signals PRESENT PERFECT (time up to now)
rows: so far, up to now, already, lately

blocks.incorrect: The company has launched its first product in 2009.
blocks.correct: The company launched its first product in 2009.

blocks.incorrect: Since 2020, remote work became far more common.
blocks.correct: Since 2020, remote work has become far more common.

blocks.bn: “আমি দেখেছিলাম” আর “আমি দেখেছি” প্রায় এক শোনালেও, নির্দিষ্ট শেষ সময় (in 2010, last year) থাকলে past simple; since / for / recently থাকলে present perfect।

blocks.title: Task 1 lives on this choice
blocks.body: Data tied to a past year is past simple; a trend running to the present is present perfect.

examples.Task 1: Sales fell in 2015 but have recovered every year since.

blocks.text: 2.5 Critical pair 2 · Present simple versus present continuous

items: Use the present simple for a permanent fact, a habit, or a general truth. This is the tense of most Task 2 topic sentences and of process descriptions.
Use the present continuous for something happening right now or a temporary current trend, especially with words such as currently, at the moment, these days, nowadays.

blocks.text: Present simple (general truth): Governments spend public money on healthcare. / Present continuous (current trend): The number of remote workers is increasing steadily.
Task 2 general truth: Many people believe that university education should be free. / Task 1 current trend: Demand for electric vehicles is rising sharply at present.
blocks.bn: সাধারণ সত্য বা অভ্যাস হলে present simple (Water boils at 100°C)। এখন চলছে বা সাময়িক হলে present continuous (Prices are rising now)। currently, nowadays, at the moment থাকলে সাধারণত continuous।

blocks.text: 2.6 Future forms · will, going to, and the present continuous
Three forms cover the future in IELTS:

items: will + base verb: predictions, general future facts, and decisions made at the moment of speaking. If this trend continues, sea levels will rise further.
be going to + base verb: plans already decided, and predictions based on present evidence. The government is going to introduce a carbon tax next year.
present continuous: fixed personal arrangements (mostly Speaking). I am meeting my supervisor tomorrow.

blocks.text: For Task 1 projections (a graph that forecasts into the future) and Task 2 consequences, will is the workhorse: Unless emissions are cut, the planet will face irreversible damage.
2.7 The perfect and continuous tenses you should at least recognise
You will not need all twelve constantly, but recognising them lets you read a prompt correctly and adds range when it is natural.

items: Past perfect (had + p.p.) shows which of two past events came first. Useful in Speaking Part 2 narratives. By the time the report was published, the situation had already changed.
Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing) stresses the duration of a trend reaching now. House prices have been rising steadily for over a decade.
Future perfect (will have + p.p.) projects a completed change by a future point, strong in Task 1 forecasts. By 2040, the population will have doubled.

blocks.text: Use these for genuine range, not decoration. One accurate past perfect in a Speaking narrative shows control; a forced one that does not fit reads as an error.

blocks.title: The continuous-tense trap
blocks.body: Two continuous-tense errors dominate Bangladeshi scripts. Both come from over-using the -ing form, partly because Bangla uses its continuous form more freely than English does.

error_types.label: Error type 1 · Stative verbs cannot be continuous. Some verbs describe a state, not an action in progress: know, believe, understand, mean, agree, want, need, prefer, like, love, hate, seem, appear, belong, own, contain, consist, depend, and have when it means possession.
error_types.incorrect: I am knowing the answer. / He is having two cars. / I am understanding your point now.
error_types.correct: I know the answer. / He has two cars. / I understand your point now.

error_types.label: Error type 2 · “Since” and “for” take the perfect, not the present continuous. A trend that started in the past and continues now uses the present perfect or present perfect continuous, never the plain present continuous.
error_types.incorrect: The population is increasing since 2010. / Prices are rising for the last five years.
error_types.correct: The population has increased / has been increasing since 2010. / Prices have been rising for the last five years.

blocks.bn: know, want, understand, believe, have (মালিকানা), belong এসব stative verb কখনও continuous হয় না। “I am knowing” ভুল, “I know” সঠিক। since বা for থাকলে এ পর্যন্ত চলা কাজ বোঝাতে present perfect বসে, plain present continuous নয়।

blocks.title: Time frames win or lose Task 1
blocks.body: In Writing Task 1, tense is not optional accuracy; it is the backbone of the answer. A chart with a past date range must stay in the past simple throughout. A trend that reaches the present takes the present perfect. A graph with a future projection takes will or is expected to. In Task 2, general truths and your own position sit in the present simple, while consequences and predictions take the future.

examples.Task 1: Car sales peaked in 2015, have fallen every year since, and are expected to stabilise after 2025.
examples.Task 2: Because cities continue to expand, housing shortages will worsen unless governments act now.
examples.Speaking Part 3: Attitudes have changed a great deal recently, and I think they will keep changing.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 2. Chapter 3 (Articles & Noun Types) follows.

chapters.title: Articles (A, An, The) & Noun Types
chapters.summary: The single highest-error area for Bangla speakers. Countable vs uncountable nouns, the three articles plus the zero article, a four-step proofreading decision process, and the fixed cases.

blocks.text: If you fix only one chapter in this whole book, fix this one. Articles are the single highest-error area for learners whose first language does not have them, and Bangla, Hindi, Urdu, and Nepali all lack a direct equivalent of a / an / the. This is not a minor detail. Article errors are the number one reason that otherwise strong Band 7 candidates stay stuck at Band 6.0, because the mistakes are frequent, they appear in almost every sentence, and your ear cannot catch them: your first language never trained it to.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৩-এর মূল কথা: article-ই সবচেয়ে বেশি ভুল হওয়া বিষয়, কারণ বাংলায় a / an / the-এর সরাসরি কোনো রূপ নেই। এই ভুলগুলোই ব্যান্ড ৬-এ আটকে রাখে।

blocks.text: 3.1 First, countable versus uncountable nouns
Whether you can use a / an at all depends on this distinction, so learn it before the article rules.

items: Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural form: one book, two books; a student, five students. They can take a / an in the singular.
Uncountable nouns are treated as a single mass and have no plural form and no a / an: information (never informations), water, advice.

blocks.text: The high-frequency uncountable nouns that trip up Bangladeshi candidates, worth memorising as a fixed block: information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, water, work, luggage, baggage, software, staff, homework, feedback, transport, machinery, vocabulary.
To count an uncountable noun, use a partitive phrase (a unit word) plus of:

rows: a study / a piece of research
a piece of furniture / an item of furniture
blocks.bn: কিছু noun ইংরেজিতে uncountable, যদিও বাংলায় গুনে যায় বলে মনে হয়: information, advice, furniture, equipment, research। এদের plural হয় না এবং a/an বসে না। গুনতে হলে a piece of advice, an item of furniture বলতে হয়।

blocks.text: 3.2 The three articles and the zero article
There are three articles (a, an, the) and a fourth option, no article at all, called the zero article. Every singular countable noun needs one of these four decided on purpose.
a / an (the indefinite article)

Use a / an for one, non-specific, singular, countable thing, usually mentioned for the first time. The choice between a and an depends on sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound.

items: a university, a European country (these begin with a “y” consonant sound)
an hour, an honest man (silent h, so a vowel sound)
an MBA, an X-ray (letter names beginning with a vowel sound)

blocks.text: I saw a documentary last night. (first mention, non-specific) / She wants to become an engineer. (one, non-specific)
the (the definite article)
Use the when the noun is specific: the reader or listener knows exactly which one you mean. That happens in several ways:

items: It was already mentioned: I saw a documentary. The documentary was about climate change.
There is only one of it: the sun, the government, the internet, the environment.
It is made specific by the words around it: the number of cars, the graph above, the capital of Bangladesh.
With superlatives and ordinals: the highest figure, the most important factor, the first step.

blocks.text: The chart shows the number of visitors. (both specific) / Solar power is the cleanest option available. (superlative)
the zero article (no article)
Use no article for:

items: Plural countable nouns talked about in general: Books are expensive. Cars cause pollution.
Uncountable nouns talked about in general: Water is essential. Education matters. Poverty is rising.
Most proper nouns: names of most countries, cities, people, languages: Bangladesh, Dhaka, English.

blocks.text: Education is a basic right. (general uncountable, zero article) / Cars contribute to pollution. (general plural + general uncountable)
3.3 The decision process (use this when you proofread)
When you check any singular noun, run these questions in order:

items: Is it countable? If no (uncountable), you cannot use a / an. Choose the (if specific) or zero article (if general). Stop.
If yes (countable): is it specific, known, or unique? If yes, use the.
If it is not specific and singular: use a / an (by sound).
If it is a general plural: use the zero article.
blocks.bn: proofread করার সময় প্রতিটি singular noun-এ ক্রমে প্রশ্ন করুন: (১) গুনে যায় কি না, (২) নির্দিষ্ট → the, (৩) নতুন ও একবচন হলে a/an, (৪) সাধারণ বহুবচন হলে কিছুই না।

blocks.text: 3.4 Fixed cases worth memorising
Some article choices are just fixed and should be learned as items:

items: the internet, the environment, the economy, the government, the media, the public, the world take the (treated as unique).
Superlatives always take the: the best, the largest, the most significant.
Institutions used for their purpose take zero article: go to school, go to university, go to hospital (British usage), in prison, at home. Add the only when you mean the specific building.
Countries: most take zero article (Bangladesh, France, China), but a few plural or “united/republic” names take the: the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the Philippines.
First mention then second mention: introduce with a, refer back with the. This is the classic a to the move examiners look for: The chart shows a sharp rise in 2018. The rise continued into 2019.

blocks.title: Why Bangla speakers misuse articles
blocks.body: Because Bangla has no articles at all, the category does not exist in your mental grammar, so it must be learned as an English-only system rather than translated. Three error patterns dominate.

error_types.label: Error type 1 · Omitting “the” for specific and unique things.
error_types.incorrect: Internet has changed our lives. / Government should fund school.
error_types.correct: The internet has changed our lives. / The government should fund schools.

error_types.label: Error type 2 · Using “a / an” with uncountable nouns. This is the “an advice / an information” error.
error_types.incorrect: He gave me an advice. / She did a research on it.
error_types.correct: He gave me some advice / a piece of advice. / She did research / a study on it.

error_types.label: Error type 3 · Dropping the article entirely before a singular countable noun.
error_types.incorrect: Government should take step to reduce pollution.
error_types.correct: The government should take steps to reduce pollution.

blocks.bn: uncountable noun-এর আগে a/an বসে না। “an advice”, “an information”, “a research” ভুল। বলুন “a piece of advice”, “some information”, “a study”।

blocks.title: The number one Band 6 ceiling
blocks.body: Article control is audited densely across every task. In Task 1 a single sentence can require three separate article decisions: “The chart shows the number of visitors to a museum.” In Task 2 generalisations, the pattern flips to zero article and the: “Governments should protect the environment.” Because the errors are so frequent, they are the classic thing separating a script that reads like Band 7 in ideas but scores Band 6 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy.

examples.Task 1: The graph illustrates the proportion of households with an internet connection.
examples.Task 2: Education is widely seen as the key to development, and governments should therefore fund schools properly.
examples.Speaking Part 2: The person who influenced me most was a teacher at my primary school.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 3. Chapter 4 (Prepositions & Dependency Rules) follows.

chapters.title: Prepositions & Dependency Rules
chapters.summary: Prepositions of time, place, and direction, the Task 1 data prepositions, dependent prepositions to memorise in blocks, and the direct-translation errors that mark a script as Bangladeshi.

blocks.text: Prepositions are the small words (in, on, at, by, for, to, of, from, with) that show how other words relate in time, place, and direction. They look trivial, but they carry a large share of the errors on this test, for one reason: prepositions are memorised by pattern, not by logic. There is no rule that explains why English says interested in but good at and afraid of. These are fixed collocations, and they either sound right to a native ear or they do not. For a Bangla speaker, that is a problem, because your instinct is to translate the Bangla preposition directly, and Bangla maps its relationships differently.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৪-এর মূল কথা: preposition যুক্তি নয়, প্যাটার্ন মুখস্থ করে নিতে হয়। বাংলা থেকে সরাসরি অনুবাদ করলে ভুল হয় (যেমন “discuss about”, “according to me”)।

blocks.text: 4.1 What a preposition does (zero assumption)

A preposition sits before a noun or pronoun and shows a relationship: the book is on the table (place), the meeting is at three (time), she walked into the room (direction). The noun after it is called its object. One key rule you already met in the tenses chapter returns here: after a preposition, a verb always takes the -ing form, never the infinitive. Interested in studying, responsible for managing, capable of solving.
4.2 Prepositions of time · in, on, at, and their neighbours
The three core time prepositions follow a “zooming in” logic, from long periods to exact points.

rows: months, years, seasons, centuries, long periods
in July, in 2020, in winter, in the 1990s
on Monday, on 5 May, on weekdays
at 5 p.m., at night, at the weekend, at the start

blocks.text: Other time prepositions that matter for IELTS:

items: since + a starting point (goes with the present perfect): since 2010, since January.
for + a length of time: for five years, for a decade.
during + a period (when something happens within it): during the 1990s, during the recession.
by + a deadline (not later than): by 2030, by the end of the decade.
from … to / until + a span: from 2000 to 2010, until 2015.

blocks.incorrect: In Monday the shop is closed. / The population grew since five years.
blocks.correct: On Monday the shop is closed. / The population grew for five years.

blocks.text: 4.3 Prepositions of place and direction

items: in = inside a space or area: in the room, in Dhaka, in the world.
on = on a surface or line: on the wall, on the coast, on the second floor.
at = at a specific point or place: at the station, at the top, at home.
into / onto / to show movement or direction: walk into the room, climb onto the roof, go to work.

blocks.text: The figures are shown in the chart, on the vertical axis, at the top of the page.
4.4 The Task 1 data prepositions (memorise as fixed phrases)
These combinations describe movement and quantity on a graph. They are non-negotiable in Writing Task 1, and examiners expect every one of them to be exact.

rows: a range or a time span

blocks.incorrect: Sales increased with 20 per cent and reached to a peak in June.
blocks.correct: Sales increased by 20 per cent and reached a peak in June.
blocks.why: “increase by” a percentage; “reach a peak” takes no preposition after “reach.”

blocks.text: A single strong Task 1 sentence often chains several of these: The price rose by five dollars, from 20 to 25, reaching a peak of 25 in March.
blocks.bn: পরিবর্তনের পরিমাণ = by; শুরু ও শেষ = from…to; নির্দিষ্ট মান = at বা of। “increased with” এবং “reached to” ভুল; সঠিক হলো “increased by” ও “reached” (কোনো preposition ছাড়াই)।

blocks.text: 4.5 Dependent prepositions (the ones after specific words)
Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are followed by a fixed preposition. There is no logic; you learn each as a unit. Memorise them in blocks and use them until they feel automatic.

rows: The policy resulted in higher costs.
The panel consists of five experts.
The essay focuses on two causes.
Families struggle to cope with rising costs.
blocks.caption: Verb + preposition

rows: Individuals are responsible for their choices.
People are more aware of the risks.
The system is capable of handling demand.
This trend is similar to the previous one.
Urban life is different from rural life.
He is good at solving problems.
The economy is dependent on exports.
The issue is related to poverty.
The course is suitable for beginners.
blocks.caption: Adjective + preposition
Noun + preposition
blocks.bn: এই collocation-গুলো যুক্তি নয়, মুখস্থ। block আকারে শিখুন: depend on, lead to, result in, responsible for, interested in, increase in, solution to।

blocks.title: Direct-translation preposition errors
blocks.body: These are the specific errors that come from translating a Bangla structure word for word. They are extremely common and instantly recognisable to an examiner, so fixing them gives a fast, visible accuracy gain.

error_types.label: discuss / enter / reach / marry take a direct object — no preposition
error_types.incorrect: discuss about the topic / enter into the room / reach to the destination / marry with her
error_types.correct: discuss the topic / enter the room / reach the destination / marry her

error_types.label: according to me / return back / comprise of / mention about / cope up with
error_types.incorrect: According to me / return back home / comprise of three parts / mention about it / cope up with
error_types.correct: In my opinion / return home / comprise three parts / mention it / cope with

blocks.bn: এই ভুলগুলো সরাসরি বাংলা অনুবাদ থেকে আসে। “নিয়ে আলোচনা” → discuss about (ভুল), সঠিক discuss। “আমার মতে” → according to me (ভুল), সঠিক in my opinion।

blocks.title: Small words, real marks
blocks.body: Prepositions affect your score in two visible places. In Writing Task 1, the data prepositions (by, from, to, of, at) are so standard that getting one wrong stands out immediately as an accuracy error. In Writing Task 2 and Speaking, the dependent prepositions (depend on, lead to, responsible for, solution to) and the direct-translation errors (discuss about, according to me) separate controlled from uncontrolled English. Because these are collocations, correct ones also lift your Lexical Resource score, so the payoff is double.

examples.Task 1: Unemployment rose by four points, from six to ten per cent, before falling to eight in 2015.
examples.Task 2: A lack of investment in public transport contributes to congestion and leads to higher emissions.
examples.Speaking Part 3: It really depends on the situation, but on balance I think education is the solution to most of these problems.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 4, and of Module 1. Module 2 (Band 7.0+ Complex Structures), Chapter 5 follows.

chapters.title: Complex Sentences & Subordinate Clauses
chapters.summary: The single most important structure for Band 7. Clause basics, the three sentence types, adverbial and relative clauses, the comma rule, and fixing fragments, run-ons, and comma splices.

blocks.text: Module 1 made your sentences correct. Module 2 makes them varied. This is the stage where scripts stop sounding like a list of short, safe statements and start reading like connected argument. The Band 7 descriptor for Grammatical Range and Accuracy asks for “a variety of complex structures used with some flexibility,” and this module supplies exactly that: complex sentences built from subordinate clauses, the passive voice for academic tone, and conditionals for arguing about possibilities.
blocks.bn: মডিউল ২-এর লক্ষ্য: সঠিক বাক্যকে বৈচিত্র্যময় করা। ব্যান্ড ৭-এর জন্য দরকার নানা রকম complex structure। এই মডিউল complex sentence, passive voice ও conditional দেয়, তবে Module 1-এর নির্ভুলতা ধরে রেখে।

blocks.text: The complex sentence is the single most important structure for reaching Band 7, because it is the clearest signal of range. It lets you show a logical relationship between two ideas (contrast, reason, condition, time) inside one controlled sentence, instead of two short disconnected ones.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৫-এর মূল কথা: complex sentence-ই ব্যান্ড ৭-এ পৌঁছানোর সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কাঠামো, কারণ এটি range দেয় এবং দুটি ধারণার মধ্যে যুক্তিসঙ্গত সম্পর্ক একটি বাক্যে বাঁধে।

blocks.text: 5.1 Clause basics (start here)
A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. There are two kinds, and the whole chapter rests on telling them apart.

items: An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence: “Cities offer jobs.”

A dependent (subordinate) clause has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone, because a subordinating word at its front leaves it unfinished: “Although cities offer jobs …” This makes you wait for the rest.

blocks.text: A complex sentence joins one independent clause with at least one dependent clause: Although cities offer jobs, (dependent) they are crowded. (independent)
5.2 The three sentence types, and why complex wins marks

rows: Cities offer jobs, but they are crowded.
Although cities offer jobs, they are crowded.

blocks.text: A Band 5 script is mostly simple sentences. A Band 6 script mixes simple and compound. A Band 7 script controls complex sentences and uses a variety of them. There are two main tools: adverbial clauses (5.3) and relative clauses (5.4).
5.3 Adverbial (subordinate) clauses

An adverbial clause is a dependent clause that begins with a subordinating conjunction and shows how its idea relates to the main clause. Learn the subordinators grouped by the relationship they signal.

rows: Although it is costly, it works.
Prices rose because demand outstripped supply.
if, unless, provided that, as long as
Unless action is taken, the trend will continue.
Laws were tightened so that accidents would fall.
The cost was so high that the plan collapsed.

blocks.text: For purpose, the most useful compact form is in order to + base verb (or simply to + base verb): The city expanded the metro in order to reduce congestion.

blocks.title: The comma rule (memorise this)
blocks.text: If the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it. If it comes second, usually use no comma. Although it is costly, it works. (fronted dependent clause, comma) / It works although it is costly. (dependent clause second, no comma)
blocks.bn: dependent clause আগে বসলে পরে কমা (Although it is costly, it works); পরে বসলে সাধারণত কমা লাগে না (It works although it is costly)।

blocks.text: 5.4 Relative clauses

A relative clause adds information about a noun using a relative pronoun: who, which, that, where, whose. It lets you fold what would be two short sentences into one mature sentence, which directly serves range.

rows: Students who study abroad gain independence.
Solar power, which is clean, is expanding.
The policy that failed was expensive.
Cities where rents are high lose young workers.
Families whose income is low need support.

blocks.text: Defining versus non-defining: the comma changes the meaning
This is the part that carries the marks, and it is not decorative. The commas change what the sentence means.

items: A defining clause identifies which one and is essential. It takes no commas. Students who cheat are expelled. (only the cheating ones)
A non-defining clause adds extra, non-essential information and is fenced with commas on both sides. The students, who were tired, left early. (all of them)

blocks.text: Two rules follow from this:

items: Use that only in defining clauses. In non-defining clauses use which or who, never that. Wrong: My school, that is very old, is famous. Right: My school, which is very old, is famous.

Do not repeat the subject with a pronoun after the relative clause. This is a very common Bangladeshi error. Wrong: People which live in cities they pay more rent. Right: People who live in cities pay more rent.
blocks.bn: কমা থাকলে অতিরিক্ত তথ্য (non-defining), কমা না থাকলে কোনটি তা নির্দিষ্ট করে (defining)। that শুধু defining clause-এ; non-defining-এ which/who। এবং relative clause-এর পরে আবার they/it দিয়ে subject পুনরাবৃত্তি করবেন না।

blocks.text: Reduced relative clauses (a Band 8 touch): You can often drop the relative pronoun and the verb be to make a tighter phrase. Governments that invest in renewables … → Governments investing in renewables … / The report which was published last year … → The report published last year …

blocks.title: Fragments, run-ons, and comma splices
blocks.body: When learners first attempt complex sentences, three punctuation faults appear. All three come from not yet feeling where one clause ends and the next begins. The four legal ways to join two independent clauses: a full stop, a semicolon, a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS), or by turning one clause into a dependent clause with a subordinator. A lone comma is never one of them.

error_types.label: Fault 1 · The fragment (a dependent clause left alone).
error_types.incorrect: Because the weather was bad. The event was cancelled.
error_types.correct: Because the weather was bad, the event was cancelled.

error_types.label: Fault 2 · The run-on (two clauses with no join).
error_types.incorrect: I studied hard I failed the exam.
error_types.correct: I studied hard, but I failed the exam.

error_types.label: Fault 3 · The comma splice (two clauses joined by only a comma).
error_types.incorrect: Internet use rose rapidly, people spent more time online.
error_types.correct: Internet use rose rapidly, so people spent more time online.

blocks.bn: তিনটি ভুল: (১) fragment: dependent clause একা বসানো; (২) run-on: দুই clause কোনো যোগ ছাড়াই; (৩) comma splice: শুধু কমা দিয়ে দুই clause জোড়া। বৈধ উপায়: full stop, semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, অথবা একটিকে dependent বানানো।

blocks.title: The Band 7 range requirement
blocks.body: The phrase in the official Band 7 descriptor is “a variety of complex structures.” That word variety matters: an essay that uses only because clauses does not show range, even if every one is correct. Aim to deploy a spread across a Task 2 essay: a contrast clause (although), a reason clause (since), a conditional (if), and a relative clause or two.

examples.Task 2 (contrast + relative): While online learning widens access, it cannot fully replace the discipline that a classroom provides.
examples.Task 2 (reason + condition): Because demand continues to rise, prices will keep climbing unless supply increases.
examples.Speaking Part 3: People who grow up in cities often value convenience, whereas those from rural areas tend to prioritise community.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 5. Chapter 6 (Passive Voice & Academic Detachment) follows.

chapters.title: Passive Voice & Academic Detachment
chapters.summary: The passive across every tense you need, when to choose it, the impersonal “It is …” frames for academic detachment, and the twin pitfalls: wrong participles and overuse.

blocks.text: The passive voice turns the object of an action into the subject of the sentence, so the focus falls on what happens rather than who does it. It is one of the two or three structures that give academic writing its formal, impersonal tone, and it is essential in two specific IELTS places: the Task 1 process diagram, which is written almost entirely in the passive, and the Task 2 essay, where an impersonal register sounds more objective than a personal one. Used well, the passive lifts your tone; used everywhere, it makes writing heavy and evasive.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৬-এর মূল কথা: passive voice-এ কাজের object বাক্যের subject হয়, ফোকাস পড়ে “কী ঘটল” তার উপর, “কে করল” তার নয়। Task 1 process diagram প্রায় পুরোটাই passive, আর Task 2-তে passive নির্ব্যক্তিক academic সুর দেয়।

blocks.text: 6.1 What the passive is (zero assumption)

Compare two sentences that describe the same event: Active: Workers transport the materials. (subject = workers, the doer) / Passive: The materials are transported (by workers). (subject = materials, the receiver)

In the active voice, the subject does the action. In the passive voice, the subject receives the action, and the doer either disappears or is added at the end with by. The formula never changes: Object of the active sentence + a form of be + past participle (+ by + doer). Get the correct form of be (which carries the tense) and the past participle right and the passive is right.
6.2 The passive across the tenses
The tense lives in the be part; the past participle stays the same. This table shows the transformation for the tenses you actually need.
Notice the pattern: whatever the tense, you always end with the past participle (transported), and the be form in front of it changes to carry the time.
blocks.bn: tense থাকে be-এর মধ্যে, শেষে সবসময় past participle বসে। are transported / were transported / have been transported / will be transported / should be transported, শেষটা সবসময় transported।

blocks.text: 6.3 When to choose the passive
The passive is a tool for specific situations, not a default. Use it when:

items: The doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. New traffic laws were introduced in 2019. (who introduced them is obvious).
You want an objective, impersonal tone. It is widely believed that education reduces poverty. (more academic than “Many people believe …”)
You are describing a process. First, the raw beans are harvested. They are then dried, roasted, and ground before the coffee is packaged.

blocks.text: 6.4 Academic detachment: the impersonal “It is …” structures
A specific, high-value use of the passive is to remove “I” and “people” from a general claim, which sounds more objective. Learn these frames:

rows: People say that tourism harms the coast.
It is said that tourism harms the coast.
blocks.bn: “I / people / everyone” বাদ দিয়ে It is argued that…, It is widely believed that… ব্যবহার করলে লেখা বেশি নির্ব্যক্তিক ও academic হয়, বিশেষত Task 2-এর ভূমিকায়।

blocks.title: Get the past participle right, and do not overuse
blocks.body: The passive needs the third form of the verb, not the base form or the past simple. Bangladeshi learners often drop the participle ending. Irregular past participles must be memorised (see Appendix A): build/built, write/written, take/taken, give/given, show/shown. Also, do not overuse the passive: a whole essay in the passive reads as stiff and can hide who is responsible. In Task 2, mix passive and active.

error_types.label: Pitfall 1 · A missing or wrong past participle.
error_types.incorrect: The materials are transport to the site. / The bridge was build in 1990. / The report was wrote by the committee.
error_types.correct: The materials are transported to the site. / The bridge was built in 1990. / The report was written by the committee.

error_types.label: Pitfall 2 · Overusing the passive. The passive belongs mainly in the Task 1 process and in impersonal general claims; your arguments and opinions are usually clearer in the active.
error_types.incorrect: (whole essay in the passive)
error_types.correct: (mix passive and active; arguments in the active)

blocks.bn: (১) passive-এ verb-এর তৃতীয় রূপ (past participle) লাগে: are transported, was built, was written; base form বা past simple নয়। (২) পুরো Task 2 passive-এ লিখবেন না; passive মূলত Task 1 process ও নির্ব্যক্তিক বিবৃতিতে, argument সাধারণত active-এ পরিষ্কার।

blocks.title: Where the passive earns marks
blocks.body: Writing Task 1 process diagrams are the clearest case: because the doer of each step is irrelevant, the whole description runs in the passive present simple. A process answer that stays in the active sounds childish; the passive is expected. Writing Task 2 uses the passive more selectively, for the impersonal tone of general statements. Combined with the active for your own arguments, it shows the examiner you can control register.

examples.Task 1 process: Once the cocoa pods have been harvested, the beans are removed, fermented, and left to dry in the sun.
examples.Task 2 impersonal: It is often argued that stricter regulation is needed, although the costs are frequently underestimated.
examples.Speaking Part 3: A lot is being done to improve recycling, but more could be achieved with better public awareness.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 6. Chapter 7 (Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning) follows.

chapters.title: Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
chapters.summary: The four conditionals as a scale of reality, the first-vs-second choice that matters most in Task 2, the one rule that removes most conditional errors, and the hedging toolkit for academic caution.

blocks.text: Conditionals let you argue about possibilities: what happens if something is true, what would happen if it were, and what would have happened if the past had been different. This is the grammar of consequence and hypothesis, and it is central to Task 2, where almost every argument is really a conditional in disguise: if governments do X, then Y will follow. Alongside conditionals sits hedging, the language of caution (may, tend to, it is likely that), which stops your claims from sounding absolute and makes your writing sound measured and academic.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৭-এর মূল কথা: conditional দিয়ে সম্ভাবনা ও পরিণতি নিয়ে যুক্তি দেওয়া যায়—Task 2-এর প্রায় প্রতিটি যুক্তিই একটি conditional। পাশাপাশি hedging (may, tend to, it is likely that) দাবিকে নরম ও academic করে।

blocks.text: 7.1 The building block: two clauses

Every conditional has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). The order is free; if the if-clause comes first, it is followed by a comma. If demand rises, prices increase. = Prices increase if demand rises. The four standard conditionals differ only in the tense pattern across those two clauses, and each expresses a different degree of reality.
7.2 The four conditionals

rows: If you heat ice, it melts.
If taxes rise, consumption will fall.
If I were rich, I would fund schools.
If they had invested, the crisis would have been avoided.
blocks.caption: The four conditionals

blocks.text: Read the table as a scale of reality: zero is always true, first is realistically possible, second is imagined or unlikely, third is impossible now because the moment has passed. Choosing the right one is choosing how real you want the claim to sound.
blocks.bn: বাস্তবতার স্কেল: zero = সবসময় সত্য, first = বাস্তবিক সম্ভাবনা, second = কল্পিত/অসম্ভব, third = অতীতের অবাস্তব। সঠিক conditional বেছে নেওয়া মানে দাবিটি কতটা বাস্তব শোনাবে তা ঠিক করা।

blocks.text: A note on “were” in the second conditional: formal English uses were for all subjects (“If the government were to act …”), and this is the safer choice in Writing.
7.3 First versus second: the choice that matters most in Task 2
Most of your conditional errors and choices come down to first versus second, so drill this pair.

items: Use the first conditional for a real proposal you think is genuinely possible. If the government invests in public transport, congestion will decrease.
Use the second conditional for a hypothetical or a suggestion you are framing as imagined. If every citizen planted a tree, the city would be greener.

blocks.incorrect: If the government will raise taxes, spending falls.
blocks.correct: If the government raises taxes, spending will fall.
blocks.why: The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present simple, never “will.”

blocks.incorrect: If I would be in charge, I would ban cars.
blocks.correct: If I were in charge, I would ban cars.
blocks.why: The if-clause of a second conditional takes the past simple / “were,” never “would.”

blocks.title: The one rule that removes most conditional errors
blocks.text: Never put “will” or “would” in the if-clause. “Will” and “would” live in the result clause only. Keep the if-clause in a simple/past tense and you eliminate the most common conditional mistake in a single move.
blocks.bn: if-clause-এ কখনও will বা would বসাবেন না। will/would শুধু result clause-এ। এই একটি নিয়মই বেশিরভাগ ভুল সরায়।

blocks.text: 7.4 Mixed and inverted conditionals (a Band 8+ touch)
Two advanced moves add range when they fit naturally:

items: Mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result. If they had planned better (past), the city would not be so congested now (present).
Inverted conditional (formal, drops “if”): Had the government acted sooner, the crisis would have been avoided. = If the government had acted sooner … (You will meet inversion fully in Chapter 8.)

blocks.text: Use these once, accurately, for effect. A forced mixed conditional is worse than a clean standard one.
7.5 Hedging: the language of academic caution

Hedging means softening a claim so it is not an absolute statement. Band 5 writing is full of overstatements (always, never, everyone, will definitely). Band 8 writing qualifies its claims, which paradoxically makes them sound more credible and more academic. This is one of the fastest ways to raise the maturity of your tone.

rows: tend to, be likely to, appear to, seem to
often, generally, in many cases, to some extent, relatively
it is likely that, it appears that, there is a tendency for
many, some, a significant number of, the majority of
blocks.caption: The hedging toolkit

blocks.incorrect: Junk food always causes obesity and will destroy public health.
blocks.correct: Excessive consumption of junk food may contribute to obesity and could place a strain on public health.
blocks.why: “always causes” and “will destroy” are overstated; “may contribute” and “could place a strain” are measured.

blocks.text: Hedging is not weakness or vagueness. It is precision about how certain you are. “Immigration boosts the economy” is a claim you cannot fully prove; “Immigration can boost the economy” is one you can defend.
blocks.bn: hedging দুর্বলতা নয়—এটি নিশ্চয়তার মাত্রা স্পষ্ট করা। always, never, everyone, will definitely এড়িয়ে may, tend to, generally, the majority of ব্যবহার করলে লেখা বেশি পরিপক্ব শোনায়।

blocks.title: Conditional and overstatement errors
blocks.body: Two clusters of error dominate. The first is tense leakage in conditionals (putting will/would in the if-clause). The second is the habit of writing sweeping absolutes, which comes partly from the strength of assertion common in Bangla essay style.

error_types.label: Error type 1 · “will/would” in the if-clause.
error_types.incorrect: If the price will increase, demand will fall. / If governments would ban plastic, pollution would drop.
error_types.correct: If the price increases, demand will fall. / If governments banned plastic, pollution would drop.

error_types.label: Error type 2 · Unqualified absolutes.
error_types.incorrect: Technology always improves our lives. / Every student prefers online classes.
error_types.correct: Technology generally improves our lives. / Many students appear to prefer online classes.

blocks.bn: (১) if-clause-এ will/would দিয়ে ফেলা—সরানো। (২) always, every, never-এর মতো ঢালাও দাবি—generally, many, tend to দিয়ে নরম করা।

blocks.title: Conditionals and hedging together define Task 2 maturity
blocks.body: Task 2 rewards two things this chapter delivers. Conditionals give you the structure to argue consequences (“if this policy is adopted, then …”), which is the backbone of a body paragraph. Hedging gives you the tone to make those arguments sound reasoned rather than dogmatic. A script that combines an accurate second conditional with well-placed hedging reads as clearly Band 7-plus, because it shows both grammatical range and rhetorical control.

examples.Task 2 (first conditional): If governments subsidise clean energy, the transition away from fossil fuels is likely to accelerate.
examples.Task 2 (second + hedge): If education were entirely free, access might improve, though the burden on public finances would probably be considerable.
examples.Speaking Part 3: It tends to depend on the context, but on the whole I'd say technology has made communication easier.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 7, and of Module 2. Module 3 (Band 9.0 Masterclass), Chapter 8 follows.

chapters.title: Inversion, Cleft Sentences & Advanced Emphasis
chapters.summary: The rare, high-band emphasis structures: negative-adverbial inversion built with question word order, it-clefts and what-clefts, and the discipline of using one, accurately, rather than many.

blocks.text: Welcome to the Band 9 masterclass. Everything from here is about precision and sophistication, not correction. The structures in this module are the ones that appear naturally in the writing of highly proficient users: they are rare, they create emphasis, and they must be used sparingly and accurately. One well-placed inversion signals mastery; three forced ones signal a candidate who has memorised a trick. Quality and control, not quantity, is the entire message of Module 3.
blocks.bn: মডিউল ৩ সম্পর্কে: এখানে লক্ষ্য নির্ভুলতা ও পরিশীলন, শুধু ভুল শোধরানো নয়। এই কাঠামোগুলো কম ব্যবহার করুন, কিন্তু নির্ভুল। একটি সঠিক inversion দক্ষতা দেখায়; তিনটি জোর করে বসানো inversion বিপরীত ফল দেয়।

blocks.text: 8.1 What inversion is

Inversion means reversing the normal subject-verb order so that the verb (or auxiliary) comes before the subject, the pattern you normally only see in questions. In statements, we do it deliberately for emphasis, usually by moving a negative or limiting expression to the front of the sentence. When such an expression leads, the subject and auxiliary swap places. Normal: The government has rarely intervened. / Inverted: Rarely has the government intervened.

The mechanism is exactly the question mechanism: front the negative adverbial, then use question word order (auxiliary + subject). If there is no auxiliary, introduce do / does / did, just as in questions. Normal: The minister realised the scale of the problem only later. / Inverted: Only later did the minister realise the scale of the problem.
8.2 The trigger expressions (learn these as a set)
Inversion is triggered when one of these negative or limiting adverbials is moved to the front. Memorise the set; they are the entry ticket.

rows: Never before has the country faced such a crisis.
Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.
Not only does it cut costs, but it also saves time.
No sooner had the policy begun than it was criticised.
Hardly had the scheme started when problems emerged.
Only after / Only when / Only by
Only by investing heavily can the goal be achieved.
Under no circumstances should this be ignored.
Little did they know how costly it would be.
Not until 2015 did the figures begin to recover.
blocks.caption: Negative and limiting inversion triggers
blocks.bn: এই নেতিবাচক/সীমাবদ্ধকারী শব্দগুলো বাক্যের শুরুতে আনলেই inversion হয়: never, rarely, seldom, not only, no sooner, hardly, only when, under no circumstances, little, not until। এরপর প্রশ্নের মতো auxiliary + subject বসে।

blocks.text: 8.3 How to build an inverted sentence, step by step

items: Start with the plain sentence: The government has seldom acted so quickly.
Choose the trigger and move it to the front: Seldom …
Apply question word order (auxiliary before subject): Seldom has the government …
Complete the sentence: Seldom has the government acted so quickly.

blocks.text: If the original has no auxiliary, add do / does / did and return the main verb to its base form, exactly as when forming a question. The committee only later understood the risk. → Only later did the committee understand the risk. (not “understood”)
blocks.bn: মূল বাক্যে auxiliary না থাকলে do/does/did আনুন এবং মূল verb-কে base form-এ ফিরিয়ে আনুন: “Only later did the committee understand”, “understood” নয়।

blocks.text: 8.4 Cleft sentences: splitting for emphasis

A cleft sentence (from “cleave,” to split) divides one idea into two clauses so as to spotlight one element. It is a gentler, more common emphasis tool than inversion and is very natural in both Writing and Speaking. There are two main patterns.
It-cleft

Structure: It + is/was + the emphasised element + that/who + the rest. Plain: The lack of funding caused the failure. / Cleft: It was the lack of funding that caused the failure. (spotlight on the cause)
What-cleft (pseudo-cleft)
Structure: What + clause + is/was + the emphasised element. Plain: We need better public transport. / Cleft: What we need is better public transport. (spotlight on the solution)
The what-cleft is especially useful for opening a point emphatically in an essay or a Speaking answer: What many governments overlook is the long-term cost of inaction.
blocks.bn: cleft মানে একটি বাক্যকে দুই ভাগে ভেঙে একটি অংশে জোর দেওয়া। It was X that… (কারণে জোর), What we need is X (সমাধানে জোর)। inversion-এর চেয়ে নরম ও বেশি স্বাভাবিক।

blocks.title: Do not break agreement or over-deploy
blocks.body: The danger with these structures is not the concept but the execution. Two failures recur.

error_types.label: Failure 1 · Forgetting question word order after the trigger. The subject and auxiliary must swap; keeping normal order cancels the inversion.
error_types.incorrect: Never before the country has faced such a crisis. / Rarely politicians admit their mistakes.
error_types.correct: Never before has the country faced such a crisis. / Rarely do politicians admit their mistakes.

error_types.label: Failure 2 · Over-deployment. Using several inversions or clefts in one answer makes writing sound theatrical and unnatural. One accurate example, placed at a genuinely emphatic moment, is the goal.
error_types.incorrect: (three inversions in one paragraph)
error_types.correct: (one well-placed inversion, the rest in normal order)

blocks.bn: (১) trigger-এর পরে প্রশ্নের মতো auxiliary + subject বসাতেই হবে; স্বাভাবিক ক্রম রাখলে inversion বাতিল। (২) এক অনুচ্ছেদে একাধিক inversion/cleft দিলে কৃত্রিম শোনায়—একটিই যথেষ্ট।

blocks.title: A single inversion can lift a whole script
blocks.body: Inversion and clefts are not everyday grammar; they are the flourishes that mark the top band. Examiners looking to justify Band 8 or 9 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy look for exactly this: evidence that the candidate can produce rare, complex forms accurately and naturally. The strategic use is one inversion or cleft placed at the most important sentence of an essay or a Speaking Part 3 answer, the point you most want to emphasise. Done once, cleanly, it is a strong positive signal. Overused, it works against you.

examples.Task 2 (inversion): Not only does renewable energy reduce emissions, but it also creates long-term employment.
examples.Task 2 (what-cleft): What is often forgotten in this debate is the cost of doing nothing.
examples.Speaking Part 3 (it-cleft): It was really the support of my family that made the biggest difference.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 8. Chapter 9 (Nominalisation & Academic Density) follows.

chapters.title: Nominalisation & Academic Density
chapters.summary: The verb/adjective-to-noun transformation that defines academic register, three restructuring moves for Task 2, nominalisation as a cohesion device, and the discipline of not over-nominalising into fog.

blocks.text: Nominalisation is the process of turning a verb or an adjective into a noun, and it is the single most characteristic feature of formal academic English. Where everyday speech says “the government decided to act, and this reduced pollution,” academic writing says “the government's decision to act led to a reduction in pollution.” The information is identical; the register is transformed. Nominalisation lets you pack more meaning into fewer words, connect ideas smoothly, and adopt the impersonal, concept-focused tone that examiners associate with the highest bands.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ৯-এর মূল কথা: nominalisation মানে verb বা adjective-কে noun-এ রূপান্তর করা (decide → decision, reduce → reduction)। এটি formal academic ইংরেজির সবচেয়ে বड় বৈশিষ্ট্য—কম শব্দে বেশি তথ্য, ও নির্ব্যক্তিক সুর।

blocks.text: 9.1 The core transformation

Nominalisation converts an action word (verb) or a quality word (adjective) into a thing word (noun). Once an idea is a noun, it can become the subject of a sentence, which is what gives academic prose its abstract, concept-driven feel.

blocks.caption: Common verb→noun and adjective→noun families
blocks.bn: এই word-family জোড়াগুলো মুখস্থ করুন: reduce/reduction, grow/growth, develop/development, able/ability, poor/poverty, aware/awareness। কারণ এগুলোই Task 2-এ বারবার লাগে।

blocks.text: 9.2 How nominalisation changes a sentence
Watch the same idea move from a verb-based (personal, wordy) form to a noun-based (impersonal, dense) form.

blocks.incorrect: Because the company expanded quickly, it became difficult to manage.
blocks.correct: The company's rapid expansion led to management difficulties.
blocks.why: “expanded” becomes “expansion,” “difficult to manage” becomes “management difficulties”; the sentence is shorter and more formal.

blocks.incorrect: The government decided to invest in schools, and this improved literacy.
blocks.correct: The government's decision to invest in schools improved literacy.
blocks.why: The whole first clause collapses into a noun phrase that can act as the subject.

blocks.text: The mechanism is a three-step move you can apply on demand: find the action or quality; convert it to its noun; rebuild the sentence around that noun as subject or object.
blocks.bn: তিন ধাপ: (১) কাজ বা গুণটি খুঁজুন, (২) তাকে noun করুন, (৩) সেই noun-কে subject/object করে বাক্য গড়ুন।

blocks.text: 9.3 Three restructuring moves for Task 2

items: Turn a “because” clause into a noun subject. “Because pollution increased, health worsened” → “The increase in pollution worsened public health.”
Turn a whole event into the subject of the next sentence, for smooth linking. “The factory closed. This caused unemployment.” → “The closure of the factory caused widespread unemployment.”
Replace “X is important / X is able to” with a noun. “It is important to reduce waste” → “The reduction of waste is a priority.”

blocks.text: This second move (event → subject) is also a cohesion device: naming the previous idea as a noun (“this closure,” “such growth,” “this development”) is a sophisticated way to link paragraphs without cheap connectors like “moreover.”

blocks.title: Do not over-nominalise into fog
blocks.body: Nominalisation is powerful, but the failure mode is real: a sentence stuffed with abstract nouns becomes heavy, cold, and hard to read. The Band 9 skill is balance, using nominalisation to raise register while keeping the sentence clear. Two problems recur.

error_types.label: Problem 1 · The noun string. Chaining several abstract nouns with “of” creates an unreadable pile-up.
error_types.incorrect: The implementation of the reduction of the consumption of energy is a necessity.
error_types.correct: Reducing energy consumption is essential.

error_types.label: Problem 2 · Losing the doer entirely. Sometimes the reader needs to know who acted; total nominalisation can hide responsibility unhelpfully.
error_types.incorrect: A decision was reached and an implementation followed.
error_types.correct: The committee decided to act and then implemented the plan.

blocks.bn: অতিরিক্ত nominalisation লেখাকে ভারী ও অস্পষ্ট করে। একাধিক abstract noun “of” দিয়ে জোড়াবেন না। ভারসাম্যই ব্যান্ড ৯ দক্ষতা: register বাড়ান, কিন্তু স্পষ্টতা রাখুন।

blocks.title: The register marker of the top bands
blocks.body: Nominalisation is one of the clearest features that separates a Band 6.5 script (which reads like careful speech) from a Band 8 script (which reads like academic writing). Its two payoffs map directly onto the marking criteria: it lifts Lexical Resource, because it forces precise, formal word choice, and it lifts Coherence and Cohesion, because naming a previous idea as a noun links sentences elegantly. The instruction is to use it deliberately in your topic sentences and transitions, where density and formality matter most, while keeping your explanatory sentences clear.

examples.Task 2 topic sentence: The rapid urbanisation of developing nations has placed enormous pressure on public infrastructure.
examples.Task 2 cohesion (event → subject): This expansion, however, has come at a significant environmental cost.
examples.Task 1 summary: The overall growth in exports was matched by a comparable rise in imports.

blocks.text: End of Chapter 9, and of Module 3. Module 4 (The Full Workbook), Chapter 10, follows: full essay editing and speaking transcript polish, then the complete answer keys in Chapter 11.

chapters.title: Full Essay Editing & Speaking Transcript Polish
chapters.summary: Integrated self-editing under exam conditions: the six-pass checklist, five full flawed essays to repair from heavily to lightly flawed, and five spoken answers to raise one band without sounding scripted.

blocks.text: In every chapter so far, you fixed one error type at a time, knowing in advance what to look for. A real exam is not like that. In a real essay, every rule from Modules 1 to 3 fires at once, the errors are mixed and unlabelled, and you have to catch your own mistakes under time pressure with no key beside you. This final module trains exactly that skill: integrated self-editing. You will repair whole flawed essays containing the full range of errors, then upgrade real spoken answers from safe-but-basic to controlled-and-flexible.
blocks.bn: মডিউল ৪-এর মূল কথা: এতক্ষণ এক সময়ে এক ধরনের ভুল ঠিক করেছেন। বাস্তব পরীক্ষায় সব ভুল একসঙ্গে, লেবেল ছাড়া, সময়ের চাপে আসে। এই অধ্যায় সেই integrated self-editing শেখায়।

blocks.text: 10.1 How to use this workbook chapter

Each editing task below is a complete flawed essay or paragraph written at roughly Band 5.5 to 6.0, seeded with the specific error types you have studied. Work in a disciplined sequence rather than reading randomly for “things that look wrong.”
The self-editing checklist (run it in this order)

items: Agreement pass: check every verb against its true subject (Chapter 1).
Tense pass: check that every time frame is correct and consistent (Chapter 2).
Article pass: check every singular noun for a / an / the / zero (Chapter 3).
Preposition pass: check dependent and data prepositions (Chapter 4).
Structure pass: check for fragments, run-ons, and comma splices; look for a variety of complex sentences (Chapter 5).
Range pass: is there at least one passive, one conditional, and some hedging where appropriate (Chapters 6, 7)? Is there one accurate high-band structure (Chapters 8, 9)?
blocks.bn: সম্পাদনার ক্রম: (১) agreement, (২) tense, (৩) article, (৪) preposition, (৫) structure (fragment/run-on/comma splice), (৬) range (passive, conditional, hedging, একটি high-band কাঠামো)। এই ক্রমেই প্রতিটি pass আলাদাভাবে করুন।

blocks.text: Do a separate pass for each item. Trying to catch everything in one read is how errors slip through; specialists beat generalists when proofreading.
10.2 Full essay editing (Tasks 1 to 5)

There are five editing essays in the exercise for this chapter, graded from heavily flawed (Essay 1) to lightly flawed (Essay 5). Each has a model corrected version and a breakdown of the errors by category, so you can see which of your six passes would have caught each one. Do them in order; the later essays assume you have internalised the earlier fixes.

blocks.title: Editing mindset
blocks.text: You are not rewriting the essay into your own style. You are making the minimum corrections needed for accuracy and range while preserving the writer's meaning. That is exactly what you must do to your own script in the last five minutes of the exam.
blocks.bn: পুরো বদলে নিজের স্টাইলে লেখা নয়—অর্থ ঠিক রেখে নির্ভুলতা ও range-এর জন্য ন্যূনতম সংশোধন। পরীক্ষার শেষ পাঁচ মিনিটে ঠিক এটাই করতে হবে।

blocks.text: 10.3 Speaking transcript polish

Grammar is assessed in Speaking too, under the same Grammatical Range and Accuracy heading, but the target is different: in Speaking you need controlled flexibility in real time, not written density. The five speaking items in the exercise give you a real, basic-but-safe spoken answer and ask you to raise it one band by adding exactly the moves this course has taught, without making it sound scripted.
The upgrade toolkit for Speaking, in order of value:

items: Fix the base accuracy first: agreement, tense, and articles, since these cost the most.
Add one complex sentence: a because, although, or which clause to connect two ideas.
Add a tense contrast: move between past, present, and future to show range (“I used to … but now I … and I think I'll …”).
Add one hedging phrase: “it depends,” “I'd say,” “on the whole,” “tend to.”
Optionally, one natural cleft for emphasis: “what I really enjoy is …”

blocks.text: The aim is spoken English that is accurate and flexible, not a memorised paragraph. One natural complex sentence and one tense contrast in a Part 2 answer will do more for your score than a rehearsed idiom.
blocks.bn: Speaking-এ লক্ষ্য স্বাভাবিক নিয়ন্ত্রণ ও বৈচিত্র্য—মুখস্থ অনুচ্ছেদ নয়। আগে ভিত্তি (agreement/tense/article) ঠিক করুন, তারপর একটি complex sentence ও একটি tense-contrast যোগ করুন।

blocks.title: Why integrated editing is the real exam skill
blocks.body: Both writing tasks end with a few minutes that should be spent editing, and candidates who edit systematically routinely gain half a band in Grammatical Range and Accuracy over those who do not, because the same slips (a dropped -s, a missing article, a will in an if-clause) are both common and easy to catch on a targeted pass. In Speaking, the ability to self-correct smoothly (“the number of people were, sorry, was rising”) is itself a positive marker of control. This chapter builds the habit that turns everything you have learned into marks under exam conditions.

examples.Editing gain: A systematic six-pass edit in the last five minutes typically removes most agreement, tense, and article slips.
examples.Speaking self-correction: “They has — sorry, they have — improved a lot recently.”

blocks.text: The five editing essays and five speaking-polish items are in the exercises for this chapter. Chapter 11 then gives the complete, step-by-step answer keys for every exercise in the book.

chapters.summary: A consolidation reference rather than new drills: how to review a wrong answer, a diagnostic index of the highest-frequency errors with the single rule that fixes each, the full chapter map, and the ten-minute exam self-edit routine.

blocks.text: Every exercise in this course is self-checking: when you submit an answer, the platform shows you the correct version, the reason it is correct, and a Bengali note explaining the underlying rule. This final chapter is not another set of drills. It is a consolidation reference, the place to come back to when a mistake recurs, so you can find the one rule that fixes a whole family of errors. Use it as a diagnostic index: identify the error you keep making, then re-read the rule and the chapter it comes from.
blocks.bn: অধ্যায় ১১: এই কোর্সের প্রতিটি exercise নিজেই উত্তর, কারণ ও বাংলা নোট দেখায়। এই অধ্যায় নতুন drill নয়—এটি একটি consolidation reference। যে ভুল বারবার করছেন, সেটি খুঁজে সংশ্লিষ্ট নিয়ম আবার পড়ুন।

blocks.text: 11.1 How to review an incorrect answer
When you get an item wrong, do not simply read the correct answer and move on. Spend thirty seconds diagnosing it, because the same error type will return in your own writing.

items: Read the model answer and the reason together, so you see the rule in action, not just the fix.
Name the error type: is it agreement, tense, article, preposition, structure, or a range issue?
Go back to the source chapter for that type (the map is in 11.3) and re-read the one rule that governs it.
Write two fresh sentences of your own that apply the rule correctly. Producing the form, not just recognising it, is what moves it into your active grammar.
blocks.bn: ভুল হলে: (১) মডেল উত্তর ও কারণ একসাথে পড়ুন, (২) ভুলের ধরন নাম দিন, (৩) সংশ্লিষ্ট অধ্যায়ে ফিরে যান, (৪) নিজে দুটি নতুন বাক্য লিখুন।

blocks.text: 11.2 The highest-frequency errors, and the single rule that fixes each
These are the mistakes that appear most often in Bangladeshi scripts. If you internalise this short table, you remove the majority of your recurring errors.

rows: The verb agrees with the true subject, not the nearest noun.
Uncountable nouns take no a/an and no plural.
A finished year takes the past simple, not the present perfect.
‘Since/for’ take a perfect tense, not the present continuous.
Direct-translation prepositions: discuss X; in my opinion.
A dependent clause cannot stand alone (fragment).
Two clauses need more than a comma (comma splice).
Hedge sweeping claims: may, tend to, generally.
After a fronted negative, use question word order.
blocks.caption: Diagnostic index of recurring errors
blocks.bn: এই ছকটি সবচেয়ে বেশি হওয়া ভুলগুলো এক নজরে দেখায়। যেটি বারবার ভুল হয়, সেই row-এর নিয়ম ও অধ্যায়ে ফিরে যান।

rows: verb–subject matching, the eight tricky cases

blocks.text: 11.4 The final ten-minute exam routine

On exam day, the grammar you have built pays off only if you leave time to apply the self-edit. Reserve the last few minutes of each writing task for a targeted review, running the passes from Chapter 10 in order.

items: Task 1 (leave ~3 minutes): check every tense against the time frame of the data; check the data prepositions (by, from, to, of); check that “the number of” and “the proportion of” take singular verbs.

Task 2 (leave ~5 minutes): run agreement, article, and preposition passes; confirm no “will” sits in an if-clause; confirm you have a variety of complex sentences and at least one clean high-band structure.
Speaking (in real time): if you hear an agreement or tense slip, self-correct smoothly and move on; a clean self-correction is a sign of control, not weakness.
